newsitem.title: UK: Brick-balancing Briton sets Guinness record.
newsitem.headline: Brick-balancing Briton sets Guinness record.

text.p: Burly Briton John Evans celebrated the launch of the latest Guinness Book of Records on Monday with a world first, balancing 100 bricks on his head for 14 seconds.

"That was easy. I have the strongest neck in the world," he said after establishing the record at London Zoo, setting for the launch of the 1997 edition of the book that has now sold 82 million copies in 77 countries.

The world's fastest talker, Canadian Shaun Shannon, showed how he can read Hamlet's "To be or not to be" soliloquy in 24 seconds and boasted: "It certainly keeps the costs down when you are making long distance phone calls."
Belgian Alex Lambrecht proudly showed off his 137 face and body piercings. But he said he never takes any of his rings off. "Otherwise it would take me two hours to get ready for bed."

Australian David Huxley used a plastic model to relive pulling an 187-tonne Boeing Jumbo Jet along Sydney Airport for 54.7 metres (179 ft six inches). "The hardest thing is when they start to take off," he confessed.
The annual, launched in 1955, has an entry on itself as the world's biggest-selling copyright book. It has sold in every language from Macedonian to Icelandic.
It all began when Sir Hugh Beaver, managing director of the famous brewery, was out shooting in Ireland and got into a dispute about whether the golden plover ranked as Europe's fastest game bird.
Beaver, arguing that records invariably started pub and bar disputes the world over, decided it was time to produce the ultimate reference book for superlatives.

The book has a built-in obsolescence factor which puts it back in the bestseller lists every year. "It has sold out this year in Australia, New Zealand, Malaysia, Singapore, Canada and South Africa," said marketing director Fred Buxton.
The book no longer accepts gluttony records for health and safety reasons but retains the old ones by popular request.
"They are in for historical interest. The only record that can still be broken is how fast you can eat individual baked beans with a cocktail stick," said managing editor Liz Wyse.
She confessed to being amused and amazed by the people wanting to set records and the stunts they thought up.
"Crossing the Atlantic in a pedal boat is such a lunatic idea. And as for the picture conjured up by the American woman who tap-danced for 20 miles (32 km)...."
